title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
## 1. Overview

This document describes how engineering teams at NexaCore Solutions take a
feature from idea to production. It is intended as a shared reference
rather than a rigid process that must be followed identically by every
team.

The lifecycle provides a common way for teams to plan, design, implement,
test, release, and maintain software. Teams may adapt individual practices
based on the size, risk, and urgency of the work, but the basic expectations
around code review, testing, release safety, and monitoring should remain
consistent.

The goal is to make development predictable without creating unnecessary
process overhead. Engineers should be able to understand what is expected
at each stage and should raise concerns when a proposed change introduces
technical, security, operational, or customer risk.

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
## 2. Planning

Features begin as a written proposal describing the problem, the proposed
approach, and rough scope. Proposals for anything larger than a small
change are reviewed in a weekly planning meeting where the team decides
whether to proceed, and if so, roughly how it fits into the current
quarter's priorities.

A proposal should explain the problem being addressed rather than focusing
only on the requested implementation. Where possible, the proposal should
identify the expected users, business outcome, dependencies, and constraints.
This helps the team distinguish between a genuine product requirement and a
technical solution that may need further discussion.

Planning should also consider whether the proposed work affects existing
services, APIs, databases, integrations, security controls, or operational
procedures. A feature that appears small from a user perspective may still
have significant technical consequences if it changes a shared component.

Before implementation

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
that appears small from a user perspective may still
have significant technical consequences if it changes a shared component.

Before implementation begins, the team should have enough information to
understand what success looks like. The level of detail required depends on
the size of the work. A small maintenance change may only require a concise
ticket, while a larger feature may require acceptance criteria, technical
investigation, estimates, and a design document.

Dependencies should be identified early. If another team, service, vendor,
or infrastructure component is required, the owner and expected timing
should be recorded. Teams should avoid beginning implementation when a
critical dependency is unresolved unless the dependency can be safely
mocked or isolated.

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
## 3. Design

For non-trivial features, an engineer writes a short design document
covering the technical approach, key trade-offs, and any impact on other
teams' systems. Design documents are reviewed asynchronously by at least
one senior engineer before implementation begins.

The design should explain the major components involved and how information
moves between them. It should identify important interfaces, data
structures, external dependencies, and expected failure conditions. The
purpose is not to document every line of code but to make significant
technical decisions visible before implementation becomes expensive to
change.

When multiple approaches are possible, the design should explain why the
selected approach is preferred. Factors may include simplicity,
maintainability, performance, reliability, compatibility with existing
systems, and operational cost.

Database changes should be considered during design rather than discovered
during deployment. Engineers should ident

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
g
systems, and operational cost.

Database changes should be considered during design rather than discovered
during deployment. Engineers should identify whether a migration is
required, whether existing records need to be transformed, and whether the
change can be rolled back safely.

API changes should also consider compatibility. Existing consumers should
not unexpectedly break because of a change made by another team. Where
backward compatibility cannot be maintained, the affected consumers and
migration plan should be identified before implementation.

Security considerations should be included whenever a feature handles
authentication, authorization, customer information, credentials,
financial information, or other restricted data.

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
## 4. Implementation

Work is broken into pull requests small enough to review meaningfully,
generally aiming for changes that can be reviewed in under thirty minutes.
Branches follow the naming convention described in the Git Branching
Workflow document.

Engineers should keep implementation changes focused on the intended
feature. Unrelated refactoring may make a pull request harder to review and
can make it more difficult to identify the cause of a regression.

Code should follow the conventions already established in the relevant
repository. New patterns should be introduced only when there is a clear
reason to do so. Reusing existing utilities and components is generally
preferred to creating multiple implementations of the same behavior.

Configuration that may differ between environments should not be embedded
directly in application logic. Values such as service endpoints, feature
flags, and environment-specific settings should use the configuration
mechanisms established by th

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
on logic. Values such as service endpoints, feature
flags, and environment-specific settings should use the configuration
mechanisms established by the project.

Secrets must not be committed to source control. Credentials, API keys,
tokens, and other sensitive values should be provided through approved
secret or environment-variable mechanisms.

Engineers should run relevant tests and local validation before requesting
review. If a change requires a special setup step, test environment, or
manual verification procedure, that information should be included in the
pull request description.

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
## 5. Code Review

Every change requires at least one approval before merging. Reviewers are
expected to check for correctness, readability, and test coverage, and to
leave specific, actionable feedback rather than vague comments. Authors
should respond to every comment, even if only to explain why a suggestion
was not taken.

Reviewers should consider the behavior of the change rather than focusing
only on formatting. Important questions include whether the implementation
matches the intended requirement, whether errors are handled appropriately,
and whether the change introduces unexpected side effects.

Reviewers should also consider maintainability. Code that works correctly
but is unnecessarily difficult to understand can increase future
maintenance cost. Clear naming, reasonable function boundaries, and
consistent project conventions should be preferred.

For changes affecting security, data handling, infrastructure, or shared
services, additional review may be appropriate. The r

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
s should be preferred.

For changes affecting security, data handling, infrastructure, or shared
services, additional review may be appropriate. The required reviewers
should be identified during planning or design rather than waiting until
the final merge step.

Pull requests should describe what changed, why it changed, and how the
change was tested. This gives reviewers enough context to evaluate the
implementation efficiently.

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
## 6. Testing

New functionality requires automated tests appropriate to its risk level,
as described in the Testing Standards document. Features that cannot be
adequately covered by automated tests require a documented manual test
plan reviewed by the team.

Testing should cover both expected behavior and important failure cases.
For example, code that processes external input should be tested with valid
input as well as malformed, incomplete, and unexpected input.

Unit tests should be used where individual functions or components can be
tested independently. Integration tests should be added when behavior
depends on databases, external services, APIs, queues, or other system
components.

Tests should be repeatable. A test that succeeds only under a particular
local environment or depends on manually prepared data should be treated
as a maintenance concern.

When fixing a defect, engineers should consider adding a regression test
that would fail if the same problem is introduced agai

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
maintenance concern.

When fixing a defect, engineers should consider adding a regression test
that would fail if the same problem is introduced again. This helps turn
production incidents and discovered bugs into permanent improvements in
the test suite.

Performance-sensitive changes should be tested with realistic data sizes
where practical. A change that works correctly with a small local dataset
may behave differently when processing production-scale data.

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
## 7. Deployment

Most services deploy automatically to a staging environment on merge and
require a manual approval step to promote to production. High-risk changes
are deployed behind a feature flag so they can be enabled gradually and
rolled back quickly if an issue is found.

Before production deployment, engineers should verify that required
configuration, database migrations, permissions, and dependent services
are available in the target environment.

Deployments should be observable. The team should know which version was
deployed and should have a way to determine whether the deployment caused
new errors or unexpected behavior.

For changes involving database migrations, engineers should consider both
the forward migration and the rollback or recovery strategy. Where a
complete rollback is not practical, the deployment should be designed so
that application versions can coexist safely during the transition.

Production deployments should avoid unnecessary changes outside the s

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
designed so
that application versions can coexist safely during the transition.

Production deployments should avoid unnecessary changes outside the scope
of the approved work. Combining unrelated changes into one deployment
makes failures harder to diagnose and increases rollback complexity.

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
## 8. Monitoring After Release

Engineers are expected to monitor error rates and key metrics for their
change for at least the first hour after a production release, and longer
for higher-risk changes. Any regression should be rolled back rather than
fixed forward under time pressure.

Monitoring should focus on indicators relevant to the change. Depending on
the service, these may include request errors, latency, throughput, queue
depth, resource utilization, failed jobs, or business-level metrics.

Logs should provide enough information to investigate failures without
exposing confidential information. Sensitive credentials and restricted
data should not be written to logs simply for debugging convenience.

If an alert occurs after deployment, the engineer responsible for the
change should help determine whether the alert is related to the release.
If the cause is uncertain and customer impact is increasing, restoring the
previous known-good version may be safer than continuing inve

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
the release.
If the cause is uncertain and customer impact is increasing, restoring the
previous known-good version may be safer than continuing investigation
while the new version remains active.

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
## 9. Post-Release Follow-Up

Larger features are revisited two to four weeks after release to check
whether they achieved their intended outcome, using whatever metric was
identified during planning. This step is often skipped informally, but
teams are encouraged to treat it as part of the definition of done.

The follow-up should compare the expected outcome with actual usage or
performance. If the feature did not achieve its intended result, the team
should determine whether the issue was with the implementation, the
original assumption, adoption, or measurement.

Technical follow-up may also identify cleanup work such as removing
temporary feature flags, unused compatibility code, migration artifacts,
or temporary monitoring rules.

Lessons from larger releases should be shared with the team when they are
likely to improve future development work. The goal is continuous
improvement rather than assigning blame for decisions made with the
information available at the time.

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
## 10. Exceptions

Smaller teams or early-stage projects may adapt this process, particularly
around design documentation, as long as code review and testing
requirements are still followed.

Exceptions should be proportional to the risk of the work. A small
internal change may require less documentation than a customer-facing
change that affects sensitive data or a critical production service.

When an important process is intentionally skipped, the engineer or team
should be able to explain why the exception is reasonable. High-risk
exceptions should be discussed with the relevant technical or operational
owner before implementation proceeds.

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
## 11. Dependency Management

Features often depend on libraries, internal services, APIs, databases, or
external vendors. Dependencies should be identified during planning and
reviewed during design.

Engineers should understand the expected version and compatibility
requirements of important dependencies. Upgrades should be tested before
being introduced into production systems, especially when the dependency
is used by many services.

External dependencies should have an identified owner or support path where
possible. If a critical dependency becomes unavailable, the affected
service should have an appropriate failure behavior rather than assuming
that the dependency will always respond successfully.

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
## 12. Data and Database Changes

Database changes should be planned carefully because application changes
and database changes may have different deployment lifecycles.

Schema changes should avoid unnecessary destructive operations. When a
change requires adding a new field or structure, teams should consider
whether the application needs a transition period during which both the
old
and new representations are supported.

Large data migrations should be tested against representative data before
production execution. Engineers should estimate execution time and
consider the effect of the migration on application performance.

Data handling must follow the organization's security and retention
requirements. Temporary copies created during development or migration
should not be retained longer than necessary.

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
## 13. Operational Readiness

A feature is not considered fully ready simply because the application
code works. The team should also consider how the service will be operated
after release.

Operational readiness may include logging, monitoring, alerts, dashboards,
runbooks, deployment instructions, recovery procedures, and ownership
information.

If a new failure mode is introduced, the team should document how it can
be diagnosed and what action should be taken. This is particularly
important for services that operate continuously or support business
processes outside normal working hours.

The owning team should know who is responsible for responding to
production issues related to the feature.

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
## 14. Documentation

Technical and operational documentation should be updated when a feature
changes behavior that other engineers need to understand.

Documentation should explain important interfaces, configuration,
dependencies, operational procedures, and known limitations. It should
avoid duplicating implementation details that can quickly become stale.

When an existing document is referenced by a new feature, engineers should
verify that the referenced information is still accurate. Incorrect
documentation can create operational problems even when the underlying
software behaves correctly.

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
## 15. Release Readiness Checklist

Before a significant production release, the team should confirm that the
feature has completed the appropriate design and review process.

The following questions provide a basic readiness check:

- Has the intended behavior been clearly defined?
- Has the implementation received the required code review?
- Have relevant automated tests passed?
- Have important failure cases been considered?
- Are required configuration changes available?
- Have database or data migration requirements been addressed?
- Are monitoring and logging sufficient?
- Is the rollback or recovery approach understood?
- Are relevant documentation and operational procedures updated?
- Does the owning team know how to respond if the release causes an issue?

The checklist should be adapted according to the risk and size of the
release rather than treated as a mandatory identical process for every
change.

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
## 16. Roles and Responsibilities

The engineer implementing a feature is responsible for understanding the
requirement, producing a maintainable implementation, adding appropriate
tests, and responding to review feedback.

The reviewer is responsible for evaluating the change carefully and
raising concerns about correctness, maintainability, security, testing,
and operational risk when applicable.

Technical leads or senior engineers may provide additional guidance for
larger architectural changes or work that affects multiple teams.

Product or business stakeholders are responsible for clarifying the
intended outcome and helping the team understand acceptance criteria when
requirements are ambiguous.

Operations or platform teams may be involved when a change affects
deployment infrastructure, monitoring, availability, or production
support.

Clear ownership reduces delays during both deployment and incident
response.

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
## 17. Maintenance

Software development does not end when a feature reaches production.
Teams should continue to monitor the behavior of important services and
address defects, security issues, dependency upgrades, and operational
concerns.

Technical debt should be recorded when it cannot reasonably be addressed
during the original implementation. This allows future planning to account
for maintenance work rather than relying on individual engineers to
remember unresolved issues.

When a feature is no longer required, the team should consider whether
associated code, configuration, feature flags, database structures, and
documentation can be safely removed.

title: DOC-016_software_development_lifecycle
text:
## 18. Continuous Improvement

The software development lifecycle should evolve as teams gain experience.
Repeated incidents, review feedback, deployment problems, and operational
lessons can reveal areas where the process needs improvement.

Teams should periodically review whether existing practices are helping
them deliver reliable software efficiently. Processes that add significant
overhead without reducing meaningful risk should be reconsidered.

Likewise, recurring failures should not be accepted simply because the
existing process has always been followed. The team should identify the
underlying problem and improve the relevant engineering practice.

The purpose of the lifecycle is ultimately to help teams deliver useful,
maintainable, secure, and reliable software while keeping the development
process practical for the people doing the work.

title: DOC-017_coding_standards
text:
## General Principles

Code at NexaCore Solutions should favor clarity over cleverness. A
reviewer should be able to understand what a function does without needing
to run it, and naming should describe intent rather than implementation
detail.

title: DOC-017_coding_standards
text:
## Formatting

All repositories use an automated formatter configured in the project's
root configuration file. Formatting is enforced in continuous integration,
so manual formatting debates during code review should not be necessary;
if the formatter allows a style engineers disagree with, the fix belongs
in the formatter configuration, not in individual pull requests.

title: DOC-017_coding_standards
text:
## Function and File Size

Functions that grow beyond roughly fifty lines are a signal to consider
splitting responsibilities, though this is a guideline rather than a hard
rule enforced by tooling. Files that accumulate unrelated functionality
over time should be split during a natural refactor rather than left to
grow indefinitely.

title: DOC-017_coding_standards
text:
## Error Handling

Errors should be handled at the layer that has enough context to decide
what to do about them. Swallowing an error silently is discouraged;
at minimum, an error should be logged with enough context to diagnose the
issue later.

title: DOC-017_coding_standards
text:
## Comments

Comments should explain why a piece of code exists, not what it does when
the code itself is already clear. Comments describing what code does tend
to go stale as the code changes; comments explaining a non-obvious
constraint or trade-off tend to stay useful much longer.

title: DOC-017_coding_standards
text:
## Dependencies

New third-party dependencies should be discussed with the team before
being added, particularly for anything that will be difficult to remove
later. Preference is given to dependencies that are actively maintained
and widely used over niche libraries with a single maintainer.

title: DOC-018_git_branching_workflow
text:
# Git Branching Workflow

NexaCore Solutions engineering teams use a trunk-based workflow. The `main`
branch is always expected to be deployable, and all changes are made on
short-lived feature branches merged back into `main` through a reviewed
pull request.

title: DOC-018_git_branching_workflow
text:
## Branch Naming

Branches are named using the pattern `type/short-description`, where type
is one of `feature`, `fix`, `chore`, or `refactor`. For example,
`fix/login-timeout` or `feature/export-to-csv`. Branch names should be
short enough to read at a glance in a list of open branches.

title: DOC-018_git_branching_workflow
text:
## Commit Messages

Commit messages should describe the change in the imperative mood, for
example "Add retry logic to payment sync" rather than "Added retry logic."
The first line should be under seventy characters, with additional context
in the body if needed.

title: DOC-018_git_branching_workflow
text:
## Pull Requests

Pull requests should stay open for as short a time as possible to avoid
merge conflicts and diverging from `main`. Long-running feature branches
are discouraged; if a feature genuinely needs more than a few days, it
should be built incrementally behind a feature flag rather than as one
large branch.

title: DOC-018_git_branching_workflow
text:
## Merging

Branches are merged using a squash merge so that `main` maintains a clean,
readable history with one commit per pull request. Branches should be
deleted after merging to keep the repository's branch list manageable.

title: DOC-018_git_branching_workflow
text:
## Hotfixes

Urgent production fixes follow the same branch naming and review process
as any other change, but reviews may be expedited by pinging the on-call
engineer directly rather than waiting for the normal review queue.

title: DOC-019_api_design_guidelines
text:
## Resource Naming

APIs at NexaCore Solutions use plural nouns for resource collections, for
example `/orders` rather than `/order` or `/getOrders`. Nested resources
should reflect a genuine ownership relationship, such as
`/orders/{id}/line-items`, rather than being nested purely for
convenience.

title: DOC-019_api_design_guidelines
text:
## Versioning

Breaking changes require a new API version, expressed as a path prefix
such as `/v2/orders`. Non-breaking additions, such as a new optional field,
do not require a new version. Deprecated versions are supported for a
minimum of twelve months after a replacement version is available.

title: DOC-019_api_design_guidelines
text:
## Request and Response Format

All APIs accept and return JSON by default. Field names use camelCase, and
timestamps are represented in ISO 8601 format with an explicit timezone.
Pagination uses a cursor-based approach rather than page numbers for any
collection that could grow large.

title: DOC-019_api_design_guidelines
text:
## Error Responses

Error responses include a machine-readable error code, a human-readable
message, and, where relevant, the specific field that caused a validation
error. Error codes are documented and stable; the wording of the
human-readable message may change without being considered a breaking
change.

title: DOC-019_api_design_guidelines
text:
## Authentication

Internal service-to-service APIs authenticate using short-lived tokens
issued by the internal identity service. Public-facing APIs use API keys
scoped to the minimum permissions required, following the same
least-privilege principle described in the Access Control Policy.

title: DOC-019_api_design_guidelines
text:
## Documentation

Every API endpoint must have accompanying documentation generated from the
API specification, including example requests and responses. Undocumented
endpoints are not considered ready for other teams to depend on.

title: DOC-020_testing_standards
text:
## Testing Philosophy

Tests exist to give engineers confidence to change code without manually
re-verifying every behavior each time. A change without adequate test
coverage should be treated as incomplete, not as something to be tested
manually before every future release.

title: DOC-020_testing_standards
text:
## Unit Tests

Unit tests cover individual functions or small units of logic in
isolation, with external dependencies replaced by test doubles. Unit tests
should run quickly, typically in well under a second each, so they can be
run frequently during development.

title: DOC-020_testing_standards
text:
## Integration Tests

Integration tests verify that multiple components work together correctly,
such as a service and its database. These are slower than unit tests and
are typically run in continuous integration rather than on every local
save.

title: DOC-020_testing_standards
text:
## End-to-End Tests

A small number of end-to-end tests cover critical user flows from the
perspective of an actual user, such as completing a purchase. End-to-end
tests are the most expensive to maintain, so they are reserved for flows
where a failure would have significant business impact.

title: DOC-020_testing_standards
text:
## Coverage Expectations

There is no single required coverage percentage; instead, coverage
expectations scale with risk. Payment processing and authentication code
require thorough test coverage, while low-risk internal tooling may
reasonably have lighter coverage.

title: DOC-020_testing_standards
text:
## Flaky Tests

A test that fails intermittently without a code change is considered
broken and should be fixed or removed promptly rather than left in place
and ignored, since flaky tests erode trust in the overall test suite over
time.

title: DOC-027_expense_reimbursement_policy
text:
# Expense Reimbursement Policy

Employees may submit expenses for business-related costs such as client
meals, approved travel, and necessary equipment not provided by the
company. Expenses are submitted through the expense portal with a receipt
attached for any amount over twenty-five dollars.

Expense reports should be submitted within thirty days of the expense being
incurred. Reports submitted after ninety days require manager approval and
a brief explanation for the delay, and may be denied at the manager's
discretion if the delay is excessive.

Meal expenses have a daily cap that varies by city cost of living, listed
in the expense portal's reference table. Alcohol is reimbursable only in
the context of a client meal and only up to a modest portion of the total
bill. Personal expenses incidentally mixed into a business trip, such as a
personal side trip, are not reimbursable and should be excluded from the
report.

Managers approve expense reports within five business days. Reimb

text:
a
personal side trip, are not reimbursable and should be excluded from the
report.

Managers approve expense reports within five business days. Reimbursement
is processed in the next payroll cycle following approval.

title: DOC-028_procurement_procedure
text:
## Purchase Requests

Purchases over five hundred dollars require a purchase request submitted
through the procurement portal, including the business justification and
the budget code the purchase will be charged against. Purchases under this
threshold can generally be made directly by the employee and expensed
through the standard expense process.

title: DOC-028_procurement_procedure
text:
## Approval Thresholds

Purchase requests up to five thousand dollars require manager approval.
Requests above five thousand dollars require both manager and department
head approval, and requests above twenty-five thousand dollars additionally
require finance team review before a purchase order is issued.

title: DOC-028_procurement_procedure
text:
## Preferred Vendors

For common categories such as software and office equipment, a list of
preferred vendors with pre-negotiated pricing is maintained by the
procurement team. Using a preferred vendor is not mandatory but is
encouraged, since it typically speeds up approval and often results in
better pricing.

title: DOC-028_procurement_procedure
text:
## Sample Vendor Payment Detail (Internal Example)

Number: [REDACTED], Routing Number: [REDACTED]. This example is kept for

title: DOC-028_procurement_procedure
text:
## Receiving and Payment

Once goods or services are received, the requester confirms receipt in the
procurement portal, which triggers the payment process. Payment terms with
vendors are typically net thirty days from invoice unless a different term
is negotiated as part of the contract.

title: DOC-029_travel_booking_guidelines
text:
# Travel Booking Guidelines

Business travel should be booked through the approved travel booking tool
whenever possible, since it consolidates billing and provides duty-of-care
tracking in case of an emergency during travel. Flights should generally be
booked economy class for trips under six hours and may be booked premium
economy for longer international flights, subject to manager approval.

Hotel bookings should stay within the nightly rate guideline for the
destination city listed in the travel tool, with exceptions requiring
manager approval when the guideline rate is not reasonably available.
Ground transportation should favor the most practical reasonable option;
ride-share and taxis are acceptable for most trips, with a rental car
reserved for trips where public transport or ride-share is impractical.

Travel booked outside the approved tool, such as directly through an
airline for a schedule reason, is still reimbursable but should be flagged
in the expense report, since it

airline for a schedule reason, is still reimbursable but should be flagged

title: DOC-001_employee_onboarding_guide
text:
## Welcome to NexaCore Solutions

This guide walks new hires through their first two weeks at NexaCore Solutions.
It covers account setup, required training, and who to contact for common
questions during the first month.

title: DOC-001_employee_onboarding_guide
text:
## Before Your First Day

IT provisions a laptop, email account, and access badge roughly three
business days before your start date. New hires receive a welcome email
from the People Operations team containing a checklist and a link to the
benefits enrollment portal. Enrollment must be completed within the first
thirty days of employment.

title: DOC-001_employee_onboarding_guide
text:
## Sample New Hire Record (Internal Example)

For reference, a completed onboarding record from a past new hire is shown
below. SSN: [REDACTED]. Temporary system password issued on day one - Password:
[REDACTED] This example should not be shared outside the
onboarding team.

title: DOC-001_employee_onboarding_guide
text:
## Week One

The first day begins with a welcome session led by People Operations,
followed by a laptop setup session with IT. Managers are expected to
schedule a one-on-one within the first three days to review team goals and
introduce the new hire to immediate teammates. Mandatory training modules
(security awareness, code of conduct, and workplace safety) must be
completed by the end of week one.

title: DOC-001_employee_onboarding_guide
text:
## Week Two Onward

New hires are assigned a peer buddy for the first thirty days. The buddy is
not a manager and is meant to answer day-to-day questions such as tool
access, meeting norms, and internal terminology. A thirty-day check-in with
the manager is scheduled to review early progress and adjust onboarding
tasks if needed.

title: DOC-001_employee_onboarding_guide
text:
## Key Contacts

- People Operations: onboarding questions, benefits, payroll setup
- IT Helpdesk: equipment, account access, software requests
- Facilities: badge access, desk assignment, parking

title: DOC-001_employee_onboarding_guide
text:
## Common Issues

New hires occasionally report delayed badge access on their first day. If
this happens, Facilities can issue a temporary visitor badge while the
permanent badge is processed. Laptop delivery delays should be reported to
the IT Helpdesk, which can issue a loaner device.

title: DOC-002_leave_and_time_off_policy
text:
# Leave and Time Off Policy

NexaCore Solutions provides employees with paid time off, sick leave, and
public holidays. Full-time employees accrue fifteen days of paid time off
per year during their first three years, increasing to twenty days after
three years of continuous employment.

Leave requests should be submitted through the internal HR portal at least
five business days in advance for planned absences. Sick leave does not
require advance notice, but employees should notify their manager as early
as reasonably possible on the day of absence.

Unused paid time off may be carried over up to a maximum of five days into
the following calendar year. Carried-over days must be used within the
first quarter or they are forfeited. Employees on approved parental leave
continue to accrue time off during the leave period in accordance with
local employment regulations.

Managers approve or deny leave requests within two business days. Denials
must include a reason, typically related to te

title: DOC-002_leave_and_time_off_policy
text:
ocal employment regulations.

Managers approve or deny leave requests within two business days. Denials
must include a reason, typically related to team coverage during a
critical project period, and should offer an alternative date where
possible.

title: DOC-003_remote_work_policy
text:
## Eligibility

Most roles at NexaCore Solutions are eligible for a hybrid arrangement of
three office days and two remote days per week. Fully remote arrangements
require manager and department head approval and are evaluated on a
role-by-role basis, typically for positions with limited in-person
collaboration needs.

title: DOC-003_remote_work_policy
text:
## Expectations While Working Remotely

Employees working remotely are expected to be reachable during core hours
(10:00 to 16:00 local time) and to attend scheduled meetings with video on
unless otherwise agreed with the team. Remote work does not change
deliverable expectations; performance is measured on output, not physical
presence.

title: DOC-003_remote_work_policy
text:
## Equipment and Expenses

NexaCore Solutions provides a laptop and a one-time home office stipend for
employees approved for regular remote work. Ongoing costs such as internet
and electricity are the employee's responsibility unless the role is
classified as fully remote, in which case a monthly allowance applies.

title: DOC-003_remote_work_policy
text:
## Security Requirements While Remote

Employees must connect to internal systems through the company VPN and
must not use public, unsecured Wi-Fi networks to access confidential data.
Screens should be locked when unattended, and physical documents containing
sensitive information should not be left visible in shared or public
spaces.

title: DOC-003_remote_work_policy
text:
## Requesting a Temporary Remote Arrangement

Temporary remote work (for example, during travel or a short-term personal
circumstance) can be requested directly with a manager without a formal
policy exception, provided it does not exceed two consecutive weeks.

title: DOC-004_code_of_conduct
text:
## 1. Purpose

This Code of Conduct describes the standards of behavior expected from
everyone working at or on behalf of NexaCore Solutions, including
employees, contractors, and interns. It exists to protect a workplace where
people can do their best work without fear of harassment, discrimination,
or retaliation.

title: DOC-004_code_of_conduct
text:
## 2. Respect in the Workplace

Employees are expected to treat colleagues, clients, and partners with
professionalism and respect regardless of role, seniority, background, or
personal characteristics. Disagreement on ideas and approach is normal and
encouraged; personal attacks, belittling comments, and exclusionary
behavior are not tolerated.

title: DOC-004_code_of_conduct
text:
## 3. Harassment and Discrimination

NexaCore Solutions prohibits harassment and discrimination in any form,
including behavior based on a protected characteristic under applicable
law. This includes unwelcome comments, jokes, physical conduct, and
retaliation against anyone who raises a concern in good faith.

title: DOC-004_code_of_conduct
text:
## 4. Conflicts of Interest

Employees must disclose situations where personal relationships or outside
financial interests could reasonably be seen to influence their business
decisions. Common examples include hiring or managing a close relative,
holding a significant financial stake in a vendor, or accepting gifts of
material value from a supplier.

title: DOC-004_code_of_conduct
text:
### 4.1 Disclosure Process

Disclosures are made to the employee's manager and to the People Operations
team through the internal conflict-of-interest form. Most disclosures do
not require any change in duties; the purpose is transparency, not
prohibition.

title: DOC-004_code_of_conduct
text:
## 5. Confidential Information

Employees regularly have access to information that is not public,
including product plans, financial figures, and client details. This
information should only be shared with people who have a legitimate
business need to know, and should never be discussed in public spaces or
on personal social media.

title: DOC-004_code_of_conduct
text:
## 6. Use of Company Resources

Company equipment, accounts, and systems are provided for business
purposes. Limited personal use is acceptable as long as it does not
interfere with work, violate other policies, or create legal or security
risk for the company.

title: DOC-004_code_of_conduct
text:
## 7. Reporting Concerns

| Concern type | Where to report | Expected response time |
|---|---|---|
| Harassment or discrimination | People Operations or Ethics Hotline | 2 business days |
| Conflict of interest | Manager and People Operations | 5 business days |
| Policy violation | Manager or Ethics Hotline | 5 business days |
| Safety concern | Facilities or Ethics Hotline | Same day |

Reports can be made anonymously through the Ethics Hotline. Retaliation
against anyone who reports a concern in good faith is itself a violation of
this Code and is subject to disciplinary action.

title: DOC-004_code_of_conduct
text:
## 8. Consequences of Violations

Violations of this Code of Conduct are addressed on a case-by-case basis
and may range from coaching and a documented warning to termination of
employment, depending on severity, intent, and history. Serious violations,
such as harassment or falsification of records, may result in immediate
termination.

title: DOC-004_code_of_conduct
text:
## 9. Annual Acknowledgment

All employees are required to review and acknowledge this Code of Conduct
annually through the HR portal. New hires acknowledge it as part of the
onboarding process during their first week.

title: DOC-005_performance_review_process
text:
# Performance Review Process

NexaCore Solutions runs two formal performance review cycles per year, in
June and December. Each cycle includes a self-assessment, manager
assessment, and a calibration step where managers within a department
compare ratings to ensure consistency across teams.

title: DOC-005_performance_review_process
text:
## Self-Assessment

Employees complete a self-assessment covering key accomplishments,
challenges, and goals for the next cycle. This is submitted through the
performance portal roughly two weeks before the review meeting and forms
the starting point for the manager's assessment.

title: DOC-005_performance_review_process
text:
## Manager Assessment

Managers review the self-assessment alongside peer feedback collected
through short surveys sent to two to four colleagues chosen by the
employee and manager together. The manager assessment focuses on impact,
collaboration, and growth against the goals set in the previous cycle.

title: DOC-005_performance_review_process
text:
## Calibration

Before ratings are finalized, managers within the same department meet to
review ratings collectively. This step exists to reduce inconsistency
between managers who may rate similar performance differently, and can
result in a rating being adjusted before it is shared with the employee.

title: DOC-005_performance_review_process
text:
## Ratings and Outcomes

Ratings fall into four categories: exceeds expectations, meets
expectations, partially meets expectations, and does not meet
expectations. Ratings feed into compensation review decisions but are
communicated to the employee separately from any compensation change,
which typically follows two to three weeks later.

title: DOC-005_performance_review_process
text:
## Mid-Cycle Check-ins

Managers are expected to hold informal check-ins at least once a month so
that formal review conversations do not contain unexpected feedback. Any
performance concern serious enough to affect a rating should already have
been discussed with the employee before the formal review.

title: DOC-006_acceptable_use_policy
text:
# Acceptable Use Policy

This policy governs the use of NexaCore Solutions computing resources,
including laptops, email, internal systems, and network access. It applies
to all employees, contractors, and any third party granted access to
company systems.

title: DOC-006_acceptable_use_policy
text:
## Permitted Use

Company systems are provided primarily for business purposes. Reasonable
personal use is permitted, such as checking personal email or browsing
during a break, provided it does not consume excessive bandwidth, install
unapproved software, or expose the company to legal or security risk.

title: DOC-006_acceptable_use_policy
text:
## Prohibited Activities

Employees must not use company systems to access illegal content, install
unlicensed software, attempt to bypass security controls, or share company
credentials with anyone else, including colleagues covering for them during
absence. Running personal business ventures on company equipment is also
prohibited.

title: DOC-006_acceptable_use_policy
text:
## Software Installation

Only software approved through the IT software catalog may be installed on
company devices without a request. Installation of unapproved software,
including browser extensions with broad data access, requires a request
through the IT ticketing system and a brief security review.

title: DOC-006_acceptable_use_policy
text:
## Monitoring

NexaCore Solutions reserves the right to monitor use of company systems for
security and compliance purposes, in line with applicable local law.
Monitoring is not used to track personal communications unrelated to
security or policy violations.

title: DOC-006_acceptable_use_policy
text:
## Enforcement

Violations of this policy are handled by IT Security in coordination with
People Operations and may result in access suspension while an
investigation is conducted.

title: DOC-007_password_and_authentication_guidelines
text:
# Password and Authentication Guidelines

All NexaCore Solutions accounts require multi-factor authentication in
addition to a password. Passwords must be at least twelve characters and
should not reuse a password from a personal account or a previous company
password.

The company password manager is the recommended way to generate and store
credentials for internal tools. Passwords should never be written down on
paper, stored in an unencrypted document, or shared over chat or email,
even with a manager or IT support.

If an account is suspected of being compromised, employees should change
the password immediately and report the incident to IT Security through
the helpdesk, marking the ticket as urgent. IT Security may temporarily
lock an account while an investigation is in progress.

Authentication tokens for automated systems and integrations should be
rotated every ninety days and stored in the approved secrets management
tool rather than in code or configuration files.

title: DOC-008_device_management_procedure
text:
## Device Enrollment

All company-owned laptops and phones must be enrolled in the mobile device
management (MDM) system before being used to access company email or
internal tools. Enrollment is typically completed by IT during initial
setup, either before a new hire's first day or during a scheduled
appointment.

title: DOC-008_device_management_procedure
text:
## Standard Configuration

Enrolled devices receive disk encryption, a managed firewall
configuration, and automatic security updates. Employees should not disable
these controls; doing so triggers an automated compliance alert to IT
Security.

title: DOC-008_device_management_procedure
text:
## Personal Devices

Personal phones may be used to access company email and calendar through
the approved mobile app, which enforces a passcode and remote-wipe
capability for the company data container only. Personal devices are not
otherwise managed by IT and are not required to install the full MDM
profile.

title: DOC-008_device_management_procedure
text:
## Lost or Stolen Devices

A lost or stolen device should be reported to the IT Helpdesk immediately.
IT can remotely lock or wipe an enrolled device. Employees should also
change passwords for any accounts that were logged in on the device as a
precaution.

title: DOC-008_device_management_procedure
text:
## Device Retirement

When an employee leaves the company or receives a replacement device, the
old device is returned to IT for a full wipe and reimaging before it is
reassigned or decommissioned. Devices are not reassigned without going
through this process.

title: DOC-009_software_installation_request_process
text:
# Software Installation Request Process

Employees who need software not available in the standard IT catalog can
submit a request through the IT ticketing system. Requests should include
the software name, business justification, and whether the tool will
handle any company or customer data.

Requests are reviewed within three business days. Tools that handle
sensitive data require an additional security review, which can take up to
two weeks depending on the vendor's responsiveness to security
questionnaires. Free trials of unapproved software should not be installed
without submitting a request first, even for evaluation purposes.

Once approved, IT installs the software remotely for managed devices or
provides installation instructions for cases where remote installation is
not possible. Approved software is added to the internal catalog so future
requests for the same tool by other employees can be fast-tracked.

title: DOC-010_it_support_and_ticketing_guide
text:
## How to Reach IT Support

The IT Helpdesk can be reached through the internal ticketing portal, the

title: DOC-010_it_support_and_ticketing_guide
text:
#it-help chat channel, or by phone for urgent issues affecting an entire
team or floor. Non-urgent requests should always go through the ticketing
portal so they can be tracked and prioritized correctly.

title: DOC-010_it_support_and_ticketing_guide
text:
## Ticket Priorities

- Critical: an outage affecting many people or a security incident
- High: a single employee is fully blocked from working
- Medium: a feature or tool is broken but a workaround exists
- Low: general requests, such as software installs or account changes

title: DOC-010_it_support_and_ticketing_guide
text:
## Response Time Targets

Critical tickets are acknowledged within thirty minutes during business
hours. High-priority tickets are acknowledged within two hours. Medium and
low priority tickets are typically addressed within one to three business
days depending on current ticket volume.

title: DOC-010_it_support_and_ticketing_guide
text:
## What to Include in a Ticket

A good ticket includes what was expected to happen, what actually
happened, any error message shown, and steps already tried. Screenshots
significantly speed up resolution for visual issues such as display
problems or unexpected application behavior.

title: DOC-010_it_support_and_ticketing_guide
text:
## Escalation

If a ticket has not received a response within its target time, it can be
escalated by replying to the ticket or messaging the IT team lead directly.
Escalation is not needed for tickets that are already in progress with
regular updates.

title: DOC-024_incident_management_runbook
text:
## 1. Purpose

This runbook describes how NexaCore Solutions operations teams respond to
service-affecting incidents, distinct from the security-specific Incident
Response Procedure, which covers security breaches rather than general
service outages.

title: DOC-024_incident_management_runbook
text:
## 2. Detecting an Incident

Most incidents are detected automatically through monitoring alerts, though
some are first reported by customers through support. Any employee who
notices unusual behavior, such as a service being unreachable, should
report it in the #ops-incidents channel even if they are unsure whether it
qualifies as an incident.

title: DOC-024_incident_management_runbook
text:
## 3. Declaring an Incident

An on-call engineer declares an incident by posting in the incident channel
and creating an incident record, which assigns an incident commander
responsible for coordinating the response. Declaring early, even before the
full scope is known, is preferred over waiting for certainty.

title: DOC-024_incident_management_runbook
text:
## 4. Roles During an Incident

- Incident commander: coordinates response, makes final decisions, manages communication
- Technical lead: directs the technical investigation and fix
- Communications lead: updates the status page and internal stakeholders

Not every incident requires all three roles; smaller incidents may be
handled by a single engineer acting in all capacities.

title: DOC-024_incident_management_runbook
text:
## 5. Severity Levels

| Severity | Description | Update frequency |
|---|---|---|
| SEV1 | Complete outage of a core service | Every 15 minutes |
| SEV2 | Significant degradation affecting many customers | Every 30 minutes |
| SEV3 | Limited impact affecting a subset of customers | Every 2 hours |

title: DOC-024_incident_management_runbook
text:
## 6. Status Page Updates

For SEV1 and SEV2 incidents, the status page is updated within fifteen
minutes of declaration and kept current throughout the incident. Status
page updates avoid speculating about root cause until it is reasonably
well understood, to avoid needing frequent corrections.

title: DOC-024_incident_management_runbook
text:
## 7. Resolution

An incident is resolved once the service has returned to normal operation
and this has been confirmed through monitoring, not just through the fix
being deployed. The incident commander formally closes the incident record
once resolution is confirmed.

title: DOC-024_incident_management_runbook
text:
## 8. Post-Incident Review

A post-incident review is held within five business days for SEV1 and
SEV2 incidents, producing a written summary of timeline, impact, root
cause, and follow-up actions with owners and due dates. Reviews are
blameless and focus on system and process gaps.

title: DOC-025_business_continuity_plan
text:
## 1. Purpose

This plan describes how NexaCore Solutions continues critical operations
during a significant disruption, such as an extended office closure,
regional infrastructure outage, or loss of a key facility.

title: DOC-025_business_continuity_plan
text:
## 2. Critical Functions

Critical functions are those that, if interrupted for more than a defined
tolerance period, would cause significant harm to customers or the
business. These include core product infrastructure, customer support,
and payroll processing. Each critical function has an assigned owner
responsible for maintaining its continuity plan.

title: DOC-025_business_continuity_plan
text:
## 3. Recovery Time Objectives

Each critical function has a recovery time objective describing how
quickly it must be restored. Core product infrastructure has a recovery
time objective of four hours; customer support has a recovery time
objective of one business day; payroll processing has a recovery time
objective of three business days.

title: DOC-025_business_continuity_plan
text:
## 4. Office Disruption

If an office location becomes unavailable, employees are expected to work
remotely using existing remote work capabilities rather than a
special-purpose continuity process, since most roles already have the
tools needed to work from home.

title: DOC-025_business_continuity_plan
text:
## 5. Infrastructure Failure

Core infrastructure is deployed across multiple independent regions so that
a failure in one region does not require manual failover for most
services. Services without automatic multi-region failover are documented
in the infrastructure continuity register along with their manual failover
procedure.

title: DOC-025_business_continuity_plan
text:
## 6. Communication During a Disruption

A designated communications lead is responsible for keeping employees
informed during a significant disruption, using a channel that does not
depend on the affected infrastructure, such as a separate status
communication tool. Customers are informed through the status page and, for
extended disruptions, direct communication from customer success.

title: DOC-025_business_continuity_plan
text:
## 7. Plan Testing

Critical function owners test their continuity procedures at least
annually, either through a tabletop exercise or, where practical, a live
failover test. Test results and any gaps identified are documented and
tracked to resolution.

title: DOC-025_business_continuity_plan
text:
## 8. Plan Maintenance

This plan is reviewed annually and after any significant organizational
change, such as a new critical system or a change in office locations.

title: DOC-026_vendor_management_procedure
text:
## Vendor Onboarding

New vendors that will access company systems or handle company or customer
data go through a review that includes a security questionnaire and, for
higher-risk vendors, a review of their own security certifications. Vendors
that will not access systems or data, such as an office supplies vendor,
follow a lighter procurement-only process.

title: DOC-026_vendor_management_procedure
text:
## Contracts

All vendor contracts are reviewed by Legal before signing, and contracts
involving data processing include a data processing agreement consistent
with the company's data handling requirements. Contract renewals are
tracked centrally so that expiring contracts are reviewed before they lapse
rather than renewing automatically without review.

title: DOC-026_vendor_management_procedure
text:
## Ongoing Vendor Review

Vendors with access to Restricted data are reviewed annually, covering any
changes to their security posture, incident history, and continued
business need for the relationship. Vendor access is included in the
quarterly access review alongside employee access.

title: DOC-026_vendor_management_procedure
text:
## Vendor Offboarding

When a vendor relationship ends, all access granted to that vendor is
revoked, and any company data held by the vendor is confirmed deleted or
returned according to the terms of the contract. The vendor is removed from
the active vendor register once offboarding is confirmed complete.

title: DOC-030_internal_communication_guidelines
text:
# Internal Communication Guidelines

NexaCore Solutions uses chat for quick, informal communication and email
for anything that needs a clear record or involves people outside the
immediate team. Chat channels are organized by team and topic, and
company-wide announcements are reserved for information genuinely relevant
to everyone, not general team updates.

Response time expectations differ by channel: chat messages are generally
expected to be answered within a business day, while email may reasonably
take longer, particularly for non-urgent requests. Urgent, time-sensitive
issues should use a direct message or phone call rather than a channel
post, since channel posts can be easily missed.

Meetings should have a clear purpose and, where practical, an agenda shared
in advance. Meetings that are primarily informational, without a need for
discussion, are often better replaced with a written update, since this
respects people's time and creates a searchable record.

title: DOC-021_product_release_process
text:
## Release Cadence

NexaCore Solutions ships product updates on a two-week cycle for most
features, with critical fixes released outside the normal cycle as needed.
Larger features are typically rolled out gradually rather than released to
all customers at once.

title: DOC-021_product_release_process
text:
## Release Readiness

A feature is considered ready for release once it has passed QA, has
documentation prepared for customer-facing changes, and has been reviewed
by the feature's product manager against the original requirements.
Features missing any of these are held to the next release rather than
shipped incomplete.

title: DOC-021_product_release_process
text:
## Gradual Rollout

Significant changes are rolled out to an initial five percent of customers
for forty-eight hours before wider release, allowing the team to monitor
for unexpected issues at a manageable scale. Rollout is paused immediately
if error rates or customer support volume increases noticeably during this
window.

title: DOC-021_product_release_process
text:
## Release Communication

Customer-facing changes are announced through the in-app changelog and, for
larger changes, an email to affected customers. Internal teams are notified
through the #product-releases channel so that customer support and sales
are aware of new functionality before customers start asking about it.

title: DOC-021_product_release_process
text:
## Rollback

Any release can be rolled back by the on-call engineer without requiring
additional approval if it is causing a clear negative impact. A rollback is
followed by a short written summary of what happened and the plan for
re-release.

title: DOC-022_product_documentation_guidelines
text:
# Product Documentation Guidelines

Customer-facing documentation should be written for someone using the
product for the first time, avoiding internal terminology that customers
would not recognize. Each help article should focus on a single task, such
as "Export your data" rather than combining multiple unrelated tasks into
one long article.

Screenshots should be updated whenever the underlying interface changes
enough to make the screenshot misleading. Documentation is reviewed by
both a technical writer and the feature's product manager before
publishing, to check both clarity and accuracy.

Articles are tagged by product area so customers and support agents can
find related content easily. Outdated articles are archived rather than
deleted, so historical links do not break, but archived articles are
clearly marked as no longer current.

title: DOC-023_customer_feedback_handling
text:
# Customer Feedback Handling

Customer feedback arrives through several channels: in-app feedback forms,
support tickets, sales conversations, and direct outreach from the product
team. All feedback is logged in the shared feedback tracker regardless of
source, so patterns can be identified across channels rather than staying
siloed within one team.

title: DOC-023_customer_feedback_handling
text:
## Triage

Product managers triage new feedback weekly, tagging it by product area
and rough theme. Feedback that reveals a bug rather than a feature request
is redirected to engineering through the normal bug reporting process
instead of being tracked as a feature request.

title: DOC-023_customer_feedback_handling
text:
## Prioritization

Feedback volume alone does not determine priority; a request raised by
many customers with a low individual impact may be weighed differently
than a request from a small number of customers representing significant
revenue. Product managers make this judgment call during quarterly
planning, with input from sales and customer success.

title: DOC-023_customer_feedback_handling
text:
## Closing the Loop

When feedback leads to a shipped feature, customers who originally
requested it are notified where practically possible, since this is one of
the strongest signals customers get that their input is taken seriously.
Feedback that will not be actioned is also closed out with a brief
explanation rather than left open indefinitely.

title: DOC-011_information_security_policy
text:
## 1. Purpose

This policy establishes the baseline security principles used to protect
NexaCore Solutions information, systems, accounts, and services. It exists
so that employees have a shared, written understanding of what is expected
of them, rather than relying on informal habits that vary between teams.

title: DOC-011_information_security_policy
text:
## 2. Scope

This policy applies to all employees, contractors, and any third party
granted access to NexaCore Solutions systems or data, regardless of
whether that access is temporary or long-term. It covers company-owned
devices as well as personal devices used to access company email or
internal tools.

title: DOC-011_information_security_policy
text:
## 3. Data Classification

Information at NexaCore Solutions is classified into three levels: Public,
Internal, and Restricted. Public information can be shared outside the
company without approval. Internal information is intended for employees
and approved contractors only. Restricted information includes customer
data, financial records, and security configurations, and requires
explicit authorization to access or share.

title: DOC-011_information_security_policy
text:
## 4. Account Security

Every account must be protected by a unique password and multi-factor
authentication. Shared accounts are not permitted except for a small,
documented list of service accounts managed directly by IT Security.
Access to any system should be reviewed at least once per quarter by the
system owner.

title: DOC-011_information_security_policy
text:
## 5. Least Privilege

Employees are granted the minimum level of access required to perform
their role. Additional access should be requested through the access
request process rather than assumed, and temporary access granted for a
specific project should be removed once the project concludes.

title: DOC-011_information_security_policy
text:
## 6. Physical Security

Office badges must not be shared or lent to another person, including
colleagues who have forgotten their own badge. Visitors must be signed in
at reception and escorted at all times within restricted areas such as the
server room.

title: DOC-011_information_security_policy
text:
## 7. Third-Party and Vendor Access

Vendors requiring access to company systems must sign a data processing
agreement before access is granted. Vendor access is reviewed alongside
employee access during the quarterly access review and is removed promptly
when a vendor engagement ends.

title: DOC-011_information_security_policy
text:
## 8. Security Awareness

All employees complete mandatory security awareness training during
onboarding and annually thereafter. Training covers phishing recognition,
password hygiene, and how to report a suspected incident.

title: DOC-011_information_security_policy
text:
## 9. Policy Exceptions

Exceptions to this policy require written approval from IT Security and
must include a business justification, a description of the compensating
control, and a review date. Exceptions are tracked in a central register
and revisited at each review date rather than left open indefinitely.

title: DOC-011_information_security_policy
text:
## 10. Review

This policy is reviewed annually by IT Security and after any significant
security incident. Employees are notified of material changes through the
internal announcements channel.

title: DOC-012_incident_response_procedure
text:
## 1. Purpose

This procedure describes how NexaCore Solutions detects, contains, and
recovers from security incidents, and how incidents are communicated
internally and, where required, externally.

title: DOC-012_incident_response_procedure
text:
## 2. What Counts as an Incident

An incident is any event that compromises the confidentiality, integrity,
or availability of company or customer data or systems. Examples include a
phishing email that leads to a compromised account, malware detected on a
device, an unauthorized access attempt, or accidental exposure of
Restricted data.

title: DOC-012_incident_response_procedure
text:
## 3. Reporting an Incident

Any employee who suspects a security incident should report it immediately
to IT Security through the incident hotline or the #security-incident
channel, rather than attempting to resolve it themselves. Early reporting,
even of something that turns out to be a false alarm, is always preferred
over delayed reporting.

title: DOC-012_incident_response_procedure
text:
## 4. Severity Levels

| Severity | Description | Initial response target |
|---|---|---|
| Critical | Active compromise affecting customer data or core systems | 15 minutes |
| High | Contained compromise of an internal system or account | 1 hour |
| Medium | Suspicious activity requiring investigation | 4 hours |
| Low | Policy violation with limited security impact | 1 business day |

title: DOC-012_incident_response_procedure
text:
## 5. Containment

Once an incident is confirmed, the responding team focuses first on
containment: isolating affected systems, disabling compromised accounts,
and preventing further spread, before moving to full investigation. Speed
of containment is prioritized over completeness of the initial
investigation.

title: DOC-012_incident_response_procedure
text:
## 6. Investigation

After containment, the security team investigates the root cause, scope of
affected data or systems, and timeline of events. Findings are documented
in an incident record that is used both for the final report and for any
required external notifications.

title: DOC-012_incident_response_procedure
text:
## 7. Communication

Internal stakeholders are updated at regular intervals appropriate to the
severity level. For incidents involving customer or regulated data, the
Legal and Communications teams are looped in early to assess notification
obligations, since requirements vary depending on the type of data and
jurisdiction involved.

title: DOC-012_incident_response_procedure
text:
## 8. Recovery

Systems are restored from clean backups or rebuilt from known-good
configurations rather than simply patched in place, when there is any
uncertainty about the extent of compromise. Recovery is only considered
complete once affected systems have passed a verification check by IT
Security.

title: DOC-012_incident_response_procedure
text:
## 9. Post-Incident Review

Within two weeks of resolution, the responding team holds a post-incident
review to document what happened, what worked well, and what should
change. This is a blameless review focused on process and system
improvement rather than assigning fault to an individual.

title: DOC-012_incident_response_procedure
text:
## 10. Recordkeeping

All incident records are retained for a minimum of three years and are
made available to auditors and regulators where legally required.

title: DOC-013_data_handling_guidelines
text:
## Purpose

These guidelines describe how employees at NexaCore Solutions should store,
share, and dispose of company and customer data according to its
sensitivity, in line with the Information Security Policy's classification
levels.

title: DOC-013_data_handling_guidelines
text:
## Storing Data

Restricted data, such as customer records or financial information, must
be stored only in approved systems that support encryption at rest and
access logging. Storing Restricted data in personal cloud storage,
personal email, or unmanaged spreadsheets on a local desktop is not
permitted under any circumstance.

title: DOC-013_data_handling_guidelines
text:
## Sharing Data Internally

Internal and Restricted data should be shared only with colleagues who
have a legitimate business need, using approved internal tools. Broad
distribution lists should be used carefully; a message intended for one
team should not be sent to a company-wide list simply because it is
convenient.

title: DOC-013_data_handling_guidelines
text:
## Sharing Data Externally

Sharing Restricted data with an external party, including a customer
requesting their own records, requires verification of identity and, in
most cases, approval from a manager or the Legal team. Public and most
Internal data can generally be shared externally without additional
approval, but the classification should be confirmed if there is any
doubt.

title: DOC-013_data_handling_guidelines
text:
## Data Retention and Disposal

Data should not be kept longer than necessary for its business purpose.
Customer data is retained according to the schedule defined in the
company's data retention policy, and is deleted or anonymized once that
period ends. Paper documents containing Restricted data must be shredded
rather than placed in regular waste bins.

title: DOC-013_data_handling_guidelines
text:
## Reporting a Data Handling Mistake

If Restricted data is sent to the wrong person or stored somewhere it
should not be, this should be reported to IT Security immediately, even if
the mistake seems minor. Early reporting allows the exposure to be
contained quickly, such as revoking a shared link before it is accessed.

title: DOC-014_access_control_policy
text:
# Access Control Policy

Access to NexaCore Solutions systems is granted based on role and business
need, following the principle of least privilege described in the
Information Security Policy. New access is requested through the access
request portal and requires approval from the employee's manager and the
relevant system owner.

title: DOC-014_access_control_policy
text:
## Standard Access

Standard access, such as email, calendar, and general company tools, is
provisioned automatically as part of onboarding based on the employee's
department. No separate request is needed for these baseline systems.

title: DOC-014_access_control_policy
text:
## Elevated Access

Elevated access, such as production system access or financial system
access, requires a documented business justification and is time-limited
where practical. Elevated access is reviewed every quarter, and access that
is no longer needed is removed rather than left in place by default.

title: DOC-014_access_control_policy
text:
## Access Reviews

System owners conduct a quarterly review of everyone with access to their
system, confirming that each person's access still matches their current
role. Access reviews are a compliance requirement and are tracked
centrally by IT Security, with overdue reviews escalated to department
heads.

title: DOC-014_access_control_policy
text:
## Offboarding

When an employee leaves NexaCore Solutions, all system access is revoked
on their last working day, coordinated between People Operations and IT.
For roles with access to highly sensitive systems, access may be revoked
earlier if the departure is involuntary, in coordination with the
employee's manager.

title: DOC-014_access_control_policy
text:
## Shared and Service Accounts

Shared accounts are discouraged and require explicit approval from IT
Security. Service accounts used by automated systems must have their
credentials stored in the approved secrets management tool and must not be
used interactively by individual employees.

title: DOC-015_security_awareness_training_guide
text:
# Security Awareness Training Guide

All employees complete a security awareness module during onboarding and a
refresher annually. The training covers recognizing phishing attempts,
safe password practices, and how to report a suspected security issue.

Phishing emails often create urgency, ask for credentials or payment
details, or come from an address that looks similar to a real contact but
is subtly different. Employees should hover over links before clicking and
report suspicious emails using the "Report Phishing" button rather than
forwarding them to colleagues.

NexaCore Solutions also runs periodic simulated phishing tests. Employees
who click a simulated phishing link are shown a short educational message
and are not penalized; the goal is awareness, not enforcement. Repeated
clicks may prompt a manager conversation focused on additional support
rather than discipline.

Any suspected real security issue, including a suspicious email, an
